title: How Close Will the Supermoon Get on November 24?
relatedVideoTitle: Why the Moon Is Slowly Leaving Us — and What Happens When It's Gone
description:
On November 24, 2026 at 14:54 UTC, the first of three consecutive full Supermoons reaches full phase nearly two Earth diameters closer to us than average.

Normally the Moon orbits at an average distance of 384,400 kilometres — wide enough to fit 30 Earth-sized planets side by side. During the November 24, 2026 Supermoon, its elliptical orbit brings it to about 360,755 kilometres (and 359,336 kilometres at perigee on November 25 at 21:00 UTC), or roughly 28 Earth diameters away. Look east around sunset on November 24 to watch it rise.

Watch the full Moon film next: Why the Moon Is Slowly Leaving Us — and What Happens When It's Gone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2fsQcea-voM)

Sources: NASA Science, 'Supermoons: In Depth' (science.nasa.gov/solar-system/moon/what-is-a-supermoon/); NASA Science, 'What's Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA' (2026); NASA Science, 'Moon Facts' (science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/); Ernie Wright, 'Moon Phase and Libration, 2026', NASA Scientific Visualization Studio #5587 (svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5587).

Image credits: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (Ernie Wright, SVS #5587 unlabelled plain Moon visualizations); NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter; NASA Johnson Space Center (Apollo 11 AS11-44-6667, Apollo 14 AS14-67-09386, ISS Crew Earth Observations ISS070-E-062746).
